process (Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024). The pathway has three distinct gym-based phases to
prepare the player for the subsequent grass phases. In conjunction with the grass phases,
the player will also complete more advanced gym profiling (power and reactive strength)
to ensure he is ready to resume team training (Grass Phase 4) and ultimately RTPlay (Grass
phase 5). The RTPerf pathway is completed (Grass Phase 6) when the player is deemed to
be performing at or above his previous level of performance.



Discussion
Case presentation
This previously healthy 23-year-old professional footballer was playing centre-back in
a game when he attempted to clear a ball with his left foot. He immediately experienced
an audible “pop” and pain in the adductor region of the kicking limb. The injury mechan­
ism was established as abduction, extension and external rotation of the hip prior to
kicking the ball. This particular movement places a high eccentric load on the AL
(Charnock et al., 2009), with this particular mechanism accounting for 29% of all AL
ruptures (Serner et al., 2018). After attempting the clearance, the player was unable to
continue and was immediately removed from the field for clinical evaluation.
   From the outset, the player presented with common signs and symptoms of a proximal
AL tendon rupture. Initially, clinical assessment revealed a palpable defect/dip, swelling,
and reproduction of pain in the region of the adductor origin on outer range resistance
testing (Abate et al., 2023). Within 72 hours, the player underwent Magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI), which revealed a full-thickness avulsion of the AL origin and fibrocartilage
footprint. The tendon and fibrocartilage retracted distally 3.9 cm. Accompanying this
report, the player had developed an antalgic gait and gross swelling in the adductor
region. Compared to pre-injury metrics, he was significantly impaired in hip range of
movement (flexion, abduction and internal rotation), and strength output (resisted
adduction) at 0°, 45° and 90° of hip flexion. A shared decision-making process was
undertaken by key stakeholders (doctors, orthopaedic surgeon, physiotherapists, and
coaches), with the player (Dijkstra et al., 2017) electing for a proximal AL tendon reattach­
ment with a RTPlay goal of 12–16 weeks (Best et al., 2020).



Surgical management and acute phase
Five days post-injury the player underwent surgery, where a 3–5 cm incision was made 3
cm distal to the pubic tubercle over the adductor region. The retracted AL tendon was
located and reattached to the pubic tubercle with 2 suture anchors. The subcutaneous
tissue was then closed with absorbable sutures and the skin was closed with non-
absorbable sutures (Lempainen et al., 2021). Immediately after surgery, appropriate
nutritional support, wound care, rest, and the use of cryotherapy were priorities. At 7
days postoperatively, the player was able to stop using crutches as he was able to adopt
a normal gait pattern and started a modified conditioning programme in the gym for the
upper body and the contralateral limb.
 4      A. MITCHELL AND C. HOLDING


Gym phase 1 - early loading and normal movement
During weeks 3–4 the player completed Gym Phase 1, regaining confidence in normal
movements such as squats and basic lunge patterns, first in the pool and then on land. In
the gym, regaining hip range of motion was prioritized along with the introduction of
adductor exercises using ball squeezes at 0°, 45° and 80–90° of hip flexion (Thorborg,
2023). These isometric exercises are believed to be beneficial for tendon loading and pain
reduction while promoting function (Hölmich et al., 1999). Prophylactic core stability
exercises were also introduced including basic plank positions, standing squat positions
and single leg (SL) balance-type exercises. Throughout this and subsequent phases, the
player used a numeric pain rating scale (0–10) to rate their pain, with 0 being no pain and
10 being the worst perceived pain. A score of 2 or less was considered acceptable for
exercise progression (Thorborg, 2023). Complementary to this, a global confidence rating
was used by the player to guide progression and ensure ongoing communication
between the player and the IDT (0% being no confidence and 100% being complete
confidence, with 80% required for progression) (Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024).


Gym phase 2 – reconditioning pathways
Once the player had demonstrated the basic movement patterns of Gym Phase 1, they
began Gym Phase 2, which focused on reconditioning pathways (Figure 1). This phase
lasted two and a half weeks as the player progressed through the various reconditioning
pathways in preparation for the return to running profiling in Gym Phase 3. Crucially,
adductor rehabilitation was a priority because of the surgical reattachment and its role in
football-related movements such as kicking and change of direction activities. Adductor
exercises included concentric and eccentric banded adduction, abduction, hip flexion,
and an introduction of multiplane combinations (Serner et al., 2020). Similarly, short lever
Copenhagen and standing slide board exercises were performed as pain and confidence
allowed (Serner et al., 2014). These, and the player’s overall reconditioning, were sup­
ported by exposure to the other pathways of this phase (Figure 1).
   The running preparation pathway included exercises such as wall drives, marching
patterns and low-level sled pushes. Player engagement and confidence was enhanced by
the indoor ball skills pathway, which used a stepwise approach to grading ball exercises
from seated foot contacts to 1-2 m passes, in this case. The plyometric pathway developed
the players’ ability to absorb and produce force through the stretch-shortening cycle
(SSC). This started in the pool with first double leg, and then SL exercises (squat jumps, to
countermovement to drop jump techniques), and progressed on a soft surface and,
towards the end of the phase, the normal gym floor (Mitchell et al., 2023).
   As with all the exercises in this phase, linear actions were performed first, followed by
the introduction of multidirectional patterns to gradually load the adductor region. The
injury specifics pathway inevitably included adductor progressions but also the develop­
ment of lumbo-pelvic control. Emphasis was placed on gluteal activation, avoidance of
anterior pelvic tilt and control of trunk stability to optimize load distribution through the
hip and groin region (King et al., 2018). Having progressed along the reconditioning
pathways of Gym Phase 2, the player was profiled in the return to running criteria (Gym
Phase 3) at weeks 6.5–7 to determine his readiness to run.

Gym phase 3 – return to running `criteria checklist´
From the RTPerf pathway (Figure 1), Gym Phase 3 specifically profiles the player’s ability to
begin running and the introduction of sport-specific actions in Grass Phase 1. Minimum
standards surrounding the theme of return to running have been previously documented
(Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024) and were sufficiently met by this player during weeks 6.5–7. For
example, the player completed low-intensity running preparation sessions consisting of
A-skips, B-skips, butt kicks, and ankle bounds etc., in addition to an antigravity treadmill
session at 95% of the player’s body weight. The SSC was further evaluated by plyometric
profiling, which included a hop battery (profiled by distance achieved) and force plate
jumps (profiled by eccentric, concentric and performance variables such as jump height
and reactive strength index) (Mitchell et al., 2021, 2022). Player confidence, movement
proficiency and achieving 80% of pre-injury metrics were sufficient as 100% recovery of
 6      A. MITCHELL AND C. HOLDING


SSC qualities is not possible at this point in the process. Injury specific criteria such as
adductor squeeze and hip range of motion were all within 10% of pre-injury metrics
(Figure 2), which was further supported by players’ pain levels not exceeding 2/10. At 7
weeks post-surgery, an IDT decision based on the available date allowed the player to
progress to Grass Phase 1.


Grass phase 1 – reloading and technical reintroduction
At 7 weeks, the player began Grass Phase 1 (reloading and technical reintroduction),
which included the reintroduction of running, low-intensity sport-specific skills and the
completion of power profiling in the gym (Figure 1). Using live data monitoring (Global
Positioning System [GPS]), speeds were limited to <65% of a player’s maximum and
included a combination of pitch length runs (100 m), box-to-box runs (70 m) and football
specific dribbling circuits such as the Hoff Drill (Mitchell et al., 2023). Similarly, accelera­
tions (ACCs) and decelerations (DECs) were introduced (<65% of his maximal intensity)
but were confined to small spaces (≤4 m) to limit any exposure to high-speed running
(HSR) or high-intensity ACCs and DECs (Harper et al., 2022). In the gym, the player
continued to develop his power qualities and was profiled through the hop battery (SL
horizontal and triple hop techniques) and force plate (SL countermovement and drop)
jumps. Specific to this injury, underlying strength (adductor/abductor ratio and outer
range adductor strength, obtained from isometric profiling) (Mosler et al., 2017; Serner
et al., 2020), and dynamic power (SL medial and lateral hop techniques) were targeted in
conjunction with kicking actions using a resistance band. The normalization of these,
together with a meticulous progression of kicking loads (2 m to 10 m distances) on the
grass, improved player confidence, motivation and skill retraining.


Grass phase 2 – high speed running and agility drills
At 8 weeks, the player progressed to Grass Phase 2, which involved completing HSR and
intensive agility drills, including exercises with reactive decision-making. Running speeds
were increased to <85% of the player’s maximum speed, and the intensity of ACCs and
DECs was further increased by expanding the drill distances (Figure 1) (Harper et al., 2022).
The kicking distance was systematically increased from 10 m to 40 m while closely mon­
itoring the clinical signs, symptoms, and players’ ratings of self-confidence. In the gym,
reactive strength was profiled using the SL drop jump reactive strength index. Additionally,
the adductor strength was specifically targeted for recovery from this injury. The minimum
standards that needed to be met before entering Grass Phase 3 were an inner range
adductor/abductor strength ratio of 1.2 (±0.2) N (Mosler et al., 2017), and an outer range
isometric adductor strength >3.0 (±0.7) N·m/kg (Serner et al., 2020) in addition to other
sports-specific grass and gym-based metrics (Table 1) (Mitchell & Gimpel, 2024).


Grass phase 3 – maximum speed and positional drills
From weeks 9–10, the player completed the maximum speed and positional drills of Grass
Phase 3. Drills were often enhanced by the support of a technical coach or additional players
to replicate exercises that were chaotic and highly variable by design. Defending drills

involved long passing, clearing actions and blocking movements to enhance player con­
fidence in the injury. This was matched physically by the player achieving 94% of peak speed,
96% of peak ACC intensity, and 84% of peak DEC intensity (Table 1). In the gym, he continued
to work on hip and pelvic strength exercises (King et al., 2018) and adductor-specific exercises
(Serner et al., 2020), (Table 1) seeking further improvements and for prophylaxis. At the end of
Grass Phase 3, in addition to physical characteristics, the player expressed a confidence level
of over 90% in resuming team training (Grass Phase 4) in week 10.


Comparative outcomes
At 10 weeks, the IDT decision permitted the player to return to team training (Grass
Phase 4) and was reintroduced to passing drills, phases of play and small (4 vs 4),
medium (5 vs 5 to 8 vs 8) and large practice games (9 vs 9 to 11 vs 11). The player
was also exposed to peak running speeds (97%) and peak ACCs and DECs inten­
sities (98% and 99%, respectively) in training situations, helping him to replicate
match demands. Subsequently, at 12 weeks, he completed 45 min in a U23 match
without any complications (Grass Phase 5). Further match exposure was increased
over the next 2 weeks, allowing the player to participate fully in the regular match
schedule from 14 weeks (Grass Phase 6). Complementing these grass progressions
was the continuity of gym-based strength, power and reactive strength exercises,
helping to mitigate the risk of future injury (Lauersen et al., 2014).

This case report demonstrates a successful RTPerf for a professional footballer who
sustained a rupture of the proximal AL tendon. Following an acute injury, the player
was effectively managed through surgical reattachment and adherence to a progressive
rehabilitation pathway. During the process, the player followed the RTPerf pathway, which
required him to meet phase-based clinical, psychological, and sports-specific criteria. The
RTPerf pathway was underpinned by the IDT’s shared decision-making, which aimed to
ensure a positive outcome and successful RTPerf.

    ABSTRACT
    To compare the probability of tackle success (the tackler preventing the ball‐carrier and ball from progressing towards the
    tackler try‐line) when contacting the ball‐carrier at different heights (shoulder, mid‐torso and legs) for different types of tackles
    (active, passive, smother and arm) while accounting for other tackler situational factors within seven playing levels. Video
    footage of 271 male rugby union matches were analysed across seven playing groups (Under [U] 12, n = 25 matches; U14,
    n = 35; U16, n = 39; U18 Amateur n = 39; U18 Elite n = 38; Senior Amateur, n = 40 and Senior Elite, n = 50) across England,
    New Zealand, South Africa, Portugal and USA (a total of 51,106 tackles). A multi‐level logistic regression model with tackle
    success as the outcome variable and first point of contact and type of tackle as the explanatory variables were computed.
    Included in the model as cofounders were the situational variables tackle direction, tackle sequence, number of players in the
    tackle and attacker intention. Post‐estimation marginal effects were used to calculate the probabilities (expressed as a per-
    centage %) of tackle success for each interaction between tackle type (active shoulder, smother, passive shoulder and arm) and
    the first point of contact (shoulder, mid‐torso and legs). The probability of tackle success in relation to where the ball‐carrier is
    contacted varied by tackle type and within each age group. The probabilities (Pr) for contacting the shoulder versus mid‐torso at
    the senior levels (elite and amateur) did not differ in relation to tackle success (for instance, for active shoulder tackles within
    senior elite; shoulder Pr 86% 95% CI 82–89 and mid‐torso Pr 82% 95% CI 77–86), whereas at the junior levels, contacting the
    shoulder had a higher probability than other points of contact. Active shoulder tackles had the highest probability of tackle
    success across the different playing levels across the different contact heights, whereas arm tackles had the lowest probability
    (for instance, for mid‐torso tackles within senior elite, active Pr 82% 95% CI 77–86 vs. arm Pr 69% 95% CI 64–75). Coaches and

14	Martin A. Lang1, Ross Tucker2, Suzi Edwards3, Grant L. Iverson4,5,6 and Andrew J. Gardner3*
15	
16	
17	  Abstract
18	  Background The rugby league tackle has been identified as the game event with the greatest propensity for a
19	  clinically diagnosed concussion. This study aims to replicate the work conducted in professional rugby league and
20	  rugby union by examining Head Injury Assessment (HIA) events to determine the associated tackle characteristics
21	  that increase concussion risk in sub-elite rugby league players. This comparison between competition levels is
22	  important due to the less developed physiological and tackle proficiency characteristics of sub-elite rugby league
23	  players and the fewer resources available for an on-field diagnosis, compared to the elite level of the sport.
24	  Results Tackles resulting in Head Injury Assessments (HIAs, n = 131) and 2,088 tackles that did not result in a head
25	  injury were identified and coded from one season of the 2019 Queensland Cup. The body position of both ball carrier
26	  and tackler, tackle height, and body contact areas were evaluated. The propensity for tacklers to undergo a head
27	  injury assessment was 1.49 HIAs per 1,000 tackles, equating to a 2.5-fold higher risk than that of the ball carrier (0.59
28	  HIAs per 1,000 tackles). The risk for an HIA was 2.75-fold greater when the tackler was upright (2.89 HIAs per 1,000
29	  tackles) compared to a bent-at-the-waist tackler (1.05 HIAs per 1,000 tackles). The greatest risk for the tackler and ball
30	  carrier sustaining an HIA occurred when the tackle height was high, with head-to-head contact having the greatest
31	  propensity for an HIA (44.37 HIAs per 1,000 tackles). HIA risk was also greater for both players when the ball carrier did
32	  not employ an evasion strategy (3.73 HIAs per 1,000 tackles).
33	  Conclusions The study replicates results from research in elite rugby league and rugby union. A combination of
34	  higher head contact/proximity and upright body position significantly increase an HIA risk. Tackler head position and
35	  ball carrier evasion behaviours also affect risk, suggesting that injury prevention strategies designed to reduce tackle
36	  height and improve tackle technique by focusing on head position, body position, and in a novel finding, ball carrier
37	  evasion, may reduce head injury risk in sub-elite rugby league players.

Tackle Risk Factors for Head Injury
Assessments (HIAs) in Sub-Elite Rugby League
and Recommendations for Prevention: Head
Contacts from Upright Tackles Increase the
HIA Risk to Both Ball Carrier and Tackler
Martin A. Lang1, Ross Tucker2, Suzi Edwards3, Grant L. Iverson4,5,6 and Andrew J. Gardner3*


  Abstract
  Background The rugby league tackle has been identified as the game event with the greatest propensity for a
  clinically diagnosed concussion. This study aims to replicate the work conducted in professional rugby league and
  rugby union by examining Head Injury Assessment (HIA) events to determine the associated tackle characteristics
  that increase concussion risk in sub-elite rugby league players. This comparison between competition levels is
  important due to the less developed physiological and tackle proficiency characteristics of sub-elite rugby league
  players and the fewer resources available for an on-field diagnosis, compared to the elite level of the sport.
  Results Tackles resulting in Head Injury Assessments (HIAs, n = 131) and 2,088 tackles that did not result in a head
  injury were identified and coded from one season of the 2019 Queensland Cup. The body position of both ball carrier
  and tackler, tackle height, and body contact areas were evaluated. The propensity for tacklers to undergo a head
  injury assessment was 1.49 HIAs per 1,000 tackles, equating to a 2.5-fold higher risk than that of the ball carrier (0.59
  HIAs per 1,000 tackles). The risk for an HIA was 2.75-fold greater when the tackler was upright (2.89 HIAs per 1,000
  tackles) compared to a bent-at-the-waist tackler (1.05 HIAs per 1,000 tackles). The greatest risk for the tackler and ball
  carrier sustaining an HIA occurred when the tackle height was high, with head-to-head contact having the greatest
  propensity for an HIA (44.37 HIAs per 1,000 tackles). HIA risk was also greater for both players when the ball carrier did
  not employ an evasion strategy (3.73 HIAs per 1,000 tackles).
  Conclusions The study replicates results from research in elite rugby league and rugby union. A combination of
  higher head contact/proximity and upright body position significantly increase an HIA risk. Tackler head position and
  ball carrier evasion behaviours also affect risk, suggesting that injury prevention strategies designed to reduce tackle
  height and improve tackle technique by focusing on head position, body position, and in a novel finding, ball carrier
  evasion, may reduce head injury risk in sub-elite rugby league players.

3	Christopher P. Sherwood,*y MS , Fintan Grogan,z BSc ,

8	Background: Concussions remain a major concern in football. A qualitative video review can provide contextual evidence sup-
9	porting changes in rules and coaching techniques aimed at reducing the risk of players sustaining a concussion.
10	Purpose: To identify tackling techniques and characteristics associated with concussions to the tackling player.
11	Study Design: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3.
12	Methods: A qualitative review of 51 concussions sustained by tacklers in National Football League (NFL) games between the
13	2015 and 2019 seasons as well as 96 control tackles was performed using video from multiple perspectives. For each concussive
14	case, 1 to 3 nonconcussive control tackles were matched based on player trajectory and closing speed as determined from
15	on-field player tracking data from Next Gen Stats. Cases and controls were coded for 20 different tackle techniques and char-
16	acteristics. The data were analyzed using conditional logistic regression models, and the results were expressed as odds ratios
17	(ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) as well as adjusted and unadjusted P values.
18	Results: Despite attempting to match cases and controls based on closing velocity, closing velocity was significantly associated
19	with the concussion risk in every logistic regression model. Predictors that had the greatest effect on the increased risk of con-
20	cussions were ‘‘tackler leading with helmet’’ (OR, 5.18 [95% CI, 1.87-14.33]; false discovery rate [FDR]–adjusted P = .0032) and
21	‘‘tackler primary loading’’ being the helmet as opposed to the shoulder (OR, 4.61 [95% CI, 1.41-15.05]; FDR-adjusted P = .0000).
22	Important factors associated with a reduced concussion risk were the tackler’s ‘‘head placed on correct side’’ of the ball carrier
23	(OR, 4.17 [95% CI, 1.58-11.01]; FDR-adjusted P = .0088) and ‘‘ball carrier primary loading,’’ with the torso having the lowest risk
24	relative to all other body segments.
25	Conclusion: The less a tackler involved his helmet in a tackle, the lower his risk of sustaining a concussion. This study supports
26	teaching players to place their heads on the correct side of the ball carrier (neither into the ball carrier nor into the path of the ball
27	carrier) when tackling to reduce their risk of a concussion, and players should target the torso of the ball carrier as their primary
28	contact point.

Tackle Techniques and Characteristics
Associated With a Concussion in Tackling
Players in the National Football League
Christopher P. Sherwood,*y MS , Fintan Grogan,z BSc ,
Timothy L. McMurry,§ PhD , James R. Funk,y PhD, PE , Jeff R. Crandall,y PhD,
Allen Sills,|| MD , and Gregory Tierney,{ PhD
Investigation performed at Biomechanics Consulting and Research, Charlottesville, Virginia, USA

Background: Concussions remain a major concern in football. A qualitative video review can provide contextual evidence sup-
porting changes in rules and coaching techniques aimed at reducing the risk of players sustaining a concussion.
Purpose: To identify tackling techniques and characteristics associated with concussions to the tackling player.
Study Design: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3.
Methods: A qualitative review of 51 concussions sustained by tacklers in National Football League (NFL) games between the
2015 and 2019 seasons as well as 96 control tackles was performed using video from multiple perspectives. For each concussive
case, 1 to 3 nonconcussive control tackles were matched based on player trajectory and closing speed as determined from
on-field player tracking data from Next Gen Stats. Cases and controls were coded for 20 different tackle techniques and char-
acteristics. The data were analyzed using conditional logistic regression models, and the results were expressed as odds ratios
(ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) as well as adjusted and unadjusted P values.
Results: Despite attempting to match cases and controls based on closing velocity, closing velocity was significantly associated
with the concussion risk in every logistic regression model. Predictors that had the greatest effect on the increased risk of con-
cussions were ‘‘tackler leading with helmet’’ (OR, 5.18 [95% CI, 1.87-14.33]; false discovery rate [FDR]–adjusted P = .0032) and
‘‘tackler primary loading’’ being the helmet as opposed to the shoulder (OR, 4.61 [95% CI, 1.41-15.05]; FDR-adjusted P = .0000).
Important factors associated with a reduced concussion risk were the tackler’s ‘‘head placed on correct side’’ of the ball carrier
(OR, 4.17 [95% CI, 1.58-11.01]; FDR-adjusted P = .0088) and ‘‘ball carrier primary loading,’’ with the torso having the lowest risk
relative to all other body segments.
Conclusion: The less a tackler involved his helmet in a tackle, the lower his risk of sustaining a concussion. This study supports
teaching players to place their heads on the correct side of the ball carrier (neither into the ball carrier nor into the path of the ball
carrier) when tackling to reduce their risk of a concussion, and players should target the torso of the ball carrier as their primary
contact point.
Keywords: football; video review; concussion; injury prevention

   "abstract":"The authors reviewed video of 51 NFL tackler concussions from the 2015 to 2019 seasons and 96 matched control tackles, coding 20 technique variables. Closing speed was significantly associated with concussion in every model, and the tackler leading with the helmet, helmet as primary contact or loading, and head placement across the ball carrier's path had the largest associations. Torso as the ball carrier's primary loading area had the lowest risk.",
   "tldr":"Tacklers who used their helmet, led with it, or placed their head across the ball carrier's path had higher concussion odds in matched NFL tackles. Coaching players to target the torso and keep their head on the correct side may lower risk, although closing speed was the strongest factor.",
   "methods":"Matched case-control study using a qualitative video review of 1-on-1 pass and rush tackles. Each 1 m/s increase in closing speed was associated with a roughly tenfold increase in risk, and ball-carrier torso loading had the lowest risk of the body parts coded.",

The study was funded by the NFL, and the author list includes an NFL employee and authors with consulting ties to the NFL.",

 "id":"Q46",
 "sourceFile":"Tackler and ball carrier technique during moderate and severe injuries compared with player-matched and team-matched injury free controls in elite Rugby Union.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in the text, 'Tackler and ball-carrier technique during moderate and severe injuries (≥8 days lost) compared with player-matched and team-matched injury-free controls in Elite Rugby Union', matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Case-control Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Coaching","Sports Medicine","Performance"],
 "sports":["Rugby"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Video analysis of 74 tackle-related moderate and severe injuries (at least 8 days lost; 31 tacklers, 43 ball-carriers) from the South African Currie Cup, 2014 to 2018, each compared with player-matched and team-matched injury-free tackles. Injury-causing tackles scored lower on standardised technical checklists than both the same player's injury-free tackles and teammates' injury-free tackles; for example, injured front-on tacklers scored 6.19 of 16 versus 8.90 for own controls and 9.93 for team controls.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The analysis used a single analyst, a univariate comparison without adjustment for situational factors, and checklists validated mainly for shoulder and arm tackles. Only 74 of 288 moderate and severe contact injuries could be matched to video, so the injured sample is selected.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the lower technique scores as proof that poor technique caused these injuries, when the study shows that injury-causing tackles were less technically proficient than matched uninjured tackles, not that the technique gap is the cause.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Meintjes V, Forshaw P, den Hollander S, et al. Tackler and ball-carrier technique during moderate and severe injuries (≥8 days lost) compared with player-matched and team-matched injury-free controls in Elite Rugby Union. Br J Sports Med. 2021;0:1-10.",
   "doi":"10.1136/bjsports-2020-103759",
   "abstract":"The authors scored tackler and ball-carrier technique in 74 moderate and severe (8 or more days lost) tackle injuries in the Currie Cup from 2014 to 2018. Each injury was compared with injury-free tackles by the same player and by teammates. Overall technical proficiency was significantly lower for the injury-causing event than for both control groups, for tacklers and ball-carriers, in front-on and side-on or behind tackles.",
   "tldr":"Tacklers and ball-carriers who were injured in moderate or severe tackle injuries in the Currie Cup scored lower on technique checklists than their own uninjured tackles and their teammates' uninjured tackles. The study identifies specific technique gaps that coaches can target in training.",
   "methods":"Case-control study using video from South African Rugby Union injury surveillance. For each injury, matched injury-free tackles by the same player (own controls) and by teammates (team controls) were identified within the same or most recent match, matched on tackle type, direction and role, with a target ratio of 1:5:5. A single analyst scored technical criteria on a 16-point or 11-point scale for tacklers and 14-point or 12-point scale for ball-carriers, and groups were compared with one-way ANOVA, Tukey post hoc tests and effect sizes.",
   "findings":"For front-on tackles, injured tacklers scored 6.19 of 16 (95% CI 4.89 to 7.48), compared with 8.90 for own controls and 9.93 for team controls. For side-on or behind tackles, injured tacklers scored 4.80 of 11, compared with 6.44 and 7.23. For ball-carriers, injured players scored 5.60 of 14 (front-on) and 5.17 of 12 (side-on or behind), compared with 8.08 and 8.16, and 7.39 and 7.75, respectively. Front-on tacklers who were injured were repeatedly weaker at moving from upright to a bent-at-waist position and at making shoulder contact first.",
   "limitations":"The analysis was univariate and did not adjust for player physical attributes, playing position, match context or the opponent's actions, and the authors note that technique scoring includes subjectivity. Only shoulder and arm tackles in front-on and side-on or behind direction were analysed, and 74 of 288 moderate and severe contact injuries could be matched to video. The sample comes from one domestic competition over five seasons, so the results may not generalise to other competitions.",
   "practicalImplications":"Coaches and trainers can use the listed technique gaps to design tackle training, for example upright-to-bent body position and shoulder-first contact for tacklers, and shifting the ball and protecting it in the correct arm for ball-carriers. The authors suggest building team databases of technique scores to find individual deficits.",
   "athleteDev":"The study points to specific tackler techniques (keeping the back straight with the centre of gravity ahead, head on the correct side, head up and forward, using the arms after contact, and releasing the ball carrier) and ball-carrier techniques (awareness of the tackler, shifting the ball to the correct arm, explosiveness, and going to ground to present the ball) that scored lower in injury-causing tackles.",
   "rtp":"The authors suggest that knowing which techniques a player lacks could help the return-to-contact process and reduce re-injury risk, but the study did not test this. The technique scores therefore cannot be used as a return-to-play criterion on the basis of this paper."
 }
}

   "rtp":"The authors suggest that knowing which techniques a player lacks could help the return-to-contact process and reduce re-injury risk, but the study did not test this. The technique scores therefore cannot be used as a return-to-play criterion on the basis of this paper."
 }
}

233	 ABSTRACT
234	
235	Purpose: To investigate how four types of successfully executed, legal front-on, one-on-one torso
236	
237	tackles influence the tacklers’ and ball carriers’ inertial head kinematics. Methods: A total of 455
238	
239	successful front-on, one-on-one torso tackle trials completed by 15 rugby-code players using three-
240	
241	dimensional motion capture were recorded. Tackles differed with respects to the height of the
242	
243	contact point on the ball carrier’s torso. A series of mixed general linear models were conducted.
244	
245	
246	                                                                            D
247	Results: The tackler sustained the highest peak resultant linear (p<0.001) and angular (p<0.01)
248	
249	head accelerations when contacting the lower torso to execute a ‘dominant’ tackle compared to
250	
251	
252	
253	
254	                            EP
255	mid or upper torso, although these latter tackle types had the lowest ball carrier inertial head
256	
257	kinematics. When executing a ‘smother’ tackle technique, a significant decrease in peak resultant
258	
259	
260	
261	
262	                              TE
263	linear head acceleration was observed with a vertical ‘pop’ then lock action employed, compared
264	
265	to the traditional upper torso tackling technique (p<0.001). Conclusions: Modifying the tackler’s
266	
267	engagement with a ball carrier’s torso, with respect to height and technical execution, alters the
268	
269	inertial head kinematics of the tackler and the ball carrier. The traditional thinking about optimal
270	
271	tackle technique, as instructed, may need to be re-evaluated with the mid-torso a potential
272	
273	               C
274	alternative target contact height, while changes in tackle execution may be relatively protective for
275	
276	tacklers when executing either a ‘dominant’ or ‘smother’ tackle. This study provides critical
277	
278	  C
279	scientific evidence to underpin revised coaching tackling technique interventions that might
280	
281	
282	
283	A
284	enhance player safety. Tackles in which the tackler contacts the ball carrier around the mid torso
285	
286	region, rather than lower torso, produce the lowest acceleration, and thus may contribute to
287	
288	reducing head injury risk for the tackler.
289	
290	
291	
292	Key Words: MOTION CAPTURE; HEAD; CONCUSSION; BIOMECHANICS
293	
294	
295	
296	
297	Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
298	 INTRODUCTION
299	
300	        The rugby codes are popular international collision sports. There are 6.1 million rugby
301	
302	union players globally, including 3.9 million in Europe, 1.8 million in Rugby North America, and
303	
304	1.1 million in Oceania (1). Numerous physical collisions (2) occur in game play, in which the
305	
306	defensive players (called the tacklers) attempt to prevent the attacking player (called the ball
307	
308	carrier) from scoring. Most elite-level rugby league players perform an average of 11 to 30 tackles
309	
310	
311	                                                                            D
312	per player per game (3), with some players performing up to 54 tackles per player per game (4).
313	
314	Elite rugby union players typically perform between 4 and 14 successful tackles per game (5).
315	
316	
317	
318	
319	                            EP
320	        The tackle event has the greatest risk for concussion (6-11). Approximately 15.4 [95% CI
321	
322	
323	
324	
325	                              TE
326	9.5 to 21.3](12) to 20.4 (11) concussions occurred per 1,000 player match hours in professional
327	
328	rugby union, and approximately 14.8 [95% CI 9.6 to 23.0](8) in professional rugby league (13).
329	
330	Online coaching instruction of safer tackling techniques and for reducing concussion risk is offered
331	
332	by many rugby code governing bodies [e.g., the National Rugby League (NRL) Tackle Safe (14)
333	
334	(www.playrugbyleague.com/), RugbySmart (15) (www.rugbysmart.co.nz/), and BokSmart (16)
335	
336	               C
337	(www.boksmart.com)]. The evidence informing the content of these injury reduction programmes
338	
339	
340	
341	  C
342	to reduce concussion risk is limited (17). The programmes are also often based on expert opinion
343	
344	rather than empirical evidence (16), and as a result, the tackling coaching content taught within
345	
346	
347	
348	A
349	these programmes is informed largely by coaching insight and not scientific evidence. It remains
350	
351	unknown whether or not the content underpinning these tackle interventions results in safer
352	
353	tackling and promotes player safety. For example, the evidence underpinning the NRL Tackle Safe
354	
355	(14) program is based on a small study with elite rugby union players (18) (not rugby league
356	
357	players). The manual identifies a mid-level injury danger area (i.e., ‘orange zone’) when the tackler
358	
359	
360	
361	
362	Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
363	 contacts the ball carrier at the mid torso (between the ball carrier’s top of pelvis and base of
364	
365	chest/pectorals), but the safest area or ‘green zone’ is claimed to be when the tackler contacts the
366	
367	ball carrier on the lower torso, the hip area. This colour zone system is not supported by recent
368	
369	evidence in professional rugby league (19), where the lowest propensity for HIAs was when the
370	
371	tackler contacts the ball carrier’s torso (i.e., mid-torso), and the highest propensity (excluding rare
372	
373	events with a low incidence e.g. boot) and most frequent impact sites are when the tackler contacts
374	
375	
376	                                                                            D
377	the torso either too high (i.e., upper torso, or above the sternum/chest) or low (i.e., hip area). This
378	
379	suggests that the NRL Tackle Safe program (14) may incorrectly identify the safest contact area,
380	
381	
382	
383	
384	                            EP
385	and that a reassessment of tackle education based on this colour zone system is warranted.
386	
387	
388	
389	
390	                              TE
391	        Despite 95% of concussions in professional rugby league occurring during the tackle (20),
392	
393	the mechanistic understanding of how tackling technique influences head impact is poorly
394	
395	understood. During a tackle, impulsive forces (incurred through rapid acceleration and
396	
397	deceleration) are applied either directly or indirectly to the head, transferring forces to the brain.
398	
399	These forces can result in a concussion by placing strain on tether points within the brain that may
400	
401	               C
402	lead to axonal stress, neuroinflammation, and a neurometabolic cascade (21), that may display as
403	
404	
405	
406	  C
407	post-concussion symptoms. These impulsive forces repetitively sustained but that do not lead a
408	
409	concussion diagnosis (i.e., sub-concussive impact) (22) including from tackling (23) are postulated
410	
411	
412	
413	A
414	to be linked to neurological issues, though emerging evidence remain inclusive to date (22).
415	
416	Whether the injury mechanism is a single event or culminative incidents, reducing the magnitude
417	
418	of inertial head kinematics of a single tackle or across hundreds of tackles will both achieve an
419	
420	effect to reduce the risk of concussion when tackling regardless of either mechanism.
421	
422	
423	
424	
425	Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
426	         Accurate in-game three-dimensional (3D) tackling methodologies to measure 3D head
427	
428	kinematics do not currently exist (24). In the laboratory, 3D retroreflective motion analysis is the
429	
430	gold standard for measuring 3D movement. It provides an understanding of 3D head kinematics
431	
432	during the tackle and provides an opportunity to examine the risks of head impact associated with
433	
434	various tackle techniques. However, the 3D retroreflection motion analysis tackle technique
435	
436	literature measured in the laboratory is emerging (24). The ball carrier has previously been found
437	
438	
439	                                                                            D
440	to experience greater changes in head angular velocity and angular acceleration in one-on-one,
441	
442	front-on, tackles in a upper torso, compared to a low (25) or mid/low torso (26) tackle height.
443	
444	
445	
446	
447	                            EP
448	        The objective of this study was to investigate how four types of successfully executed,
449	
450	
451	
452	
453	                              TE
454	legal front-on, one-on-one torso tackles influence the tackler’s and ball carrier’s inertial head
455	
456	kinematics. It was hypothesised that the tackle techniques (i.e., the Dominant, Torso & Stick (DTS)
457	
458	and the Smother Ball, Pop & Lock (SLP), described subsequently) that adhere most closely to
459	
460	tackles with the lowest propensity for HIAs (i.e., mid-torso)(19, 27) would result in significantly
461	
462	decreased peak head linear and angular acceleration for the tackler compared to hip area contact
463	
464	               C
465	(Dominant NRL, DNRL) or upper torso area (Smother NRL, SNRL).
466	
467	
468	
469	  C
470	METHODS
471	
472	
473	
474	A
475	Participants
476	
477	        Amateur or semi-professional healthy, uninjured, male, adult rugby league or rugby union
478	
479	players (n = 15) were recruited from grade competitions. The player characteristics of interest
480	
481	included: sport played (i.e., rugby league or rugby union), participant history in the sport(s) (i.e.,
482	
483	playing experience in years played), and highest competition level played. At the time of data
484	
485	
486	
487	
488	Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
489	 collection, each participant’s age, current competition level, and playing position(s) were recorded.
490	
491	It was deemed a sample size of 14 participants was sufficient based on using previous published
492	
493	data of the tacklers’ trunk flexion angle at contact when performing an upper and lower torso tackle
494	
495	(28). The power calculation was determined for two-tailed t-tests with an error probability and
496	
497	statistical power of 95% using G*Power software (29). Each participant provided written,
498	
499	informed consent prior to their participation. The University of Newcastle Human Research Ethics
500	
501	Committee (H-2017-0285) approved the study design and methodology.
502	                                                                            D
503	Experimental Procedures
504	
505	
506	                            EP
507	        Each data collection session involved two participants, one initially allocated the ball
508	
509	
510	
511	
512	                              TE
513	carrier role, and the other participant the tackler role. Participants provided informed consent,
514	
515	completed a questionnaire of their sporting participation, and then their anthropometric
516	
517	measurements were recorded for later input into a mathematical model (i.e., body mass, height,
518	
519	and pelvis, xyphoid, and chest depths). Standing in the anatomical position, a static measurement
520	
521	of both participants was recorded. The expert coach guided participants to perform a set of 10 trials
522	
523	               C
524	of one of four different one-on-one, front-on, torso tackle techniques (see Supplemental Digital
525	
526	
527	
528	  C
529	Content 1, Supplemental Figure 1, Schematic diagram of data collection of the 80 trials performed
530	
531	within a session, http://links.lww.com/MSS/C569) (30). The NRL coaching manual (31) was
532	
533	
534	
535	A
536	followed to guide the instruction of two tackling techniques where the tackler’s shoulder contacted
537	
538	the upper torso (SNRL) or hip area (DNRL) of the ball carrier, respectively. The other two tackling
539	
540	techniques were novel variations of the NRL tackles. They involved tacklers being instructed to
541

falsification, or inappropriate data manipulation. Research funding support from the National

Rugby League (NRL) Rugby League Research Committee (RLRC) for the examination of rugby-

style tackle techniques. Mr Kim Colyvas from the Faculty of Science (The University of

Newcastle) Statistical Support Service for his statistical methodological guidance for this study.

Mr Mathew Buchanan in assisting with this study’s data collection. Suzi Edwards declares that

they have no conflict of interest. Andrew Gardner, Ph.D. serves as a scientific advisor for hitIQ,

Ltd. He has a clinical practice in neuropsychology involving individuals who have sustained sport-

related concussion (including current and former athletes). He has been a contracted concussion

               C
consultant to Rugby Australia (2016-2020). He has received travel funding or been reimbursed by



  C
professional sporting bodies, and commercial organizations for discussing or presenting sport-

related concussion research at meetings, scientific conferences, workshops, and symposiums. He



A
has received research funding from the National Rugby League (NRL) for the Retired Players

Brain Health research program. Previous grant funding includes the NSW Sporting Injuries

Committee, the Brain Foundation (Australia), an Australian-American Fulbright Commission

Postdoctoral Award, a Hunter New England Local Health District, Research, Innovation and

Partnerships Health Research & Translation Centre and Clinical Research Fellowship Scheme, and

 the Hunter Medical Research Institute (HMRI), supported by Jennie Thomas, and the HMRI,

supported by Anne Greaves. Ross Tucker is a research consultant to World Rugby (Pty) Ltd, the

governing body for Rugby Union globally. Grant Iverson serves as a scientific advisor for

NanoDx™ (formerly BioDirection, Inc.), Sway Operations, LLC, and Highmark, Inc. He has a

clinical and consulting practice in forensic neuropsychology, including expert testimony,

involving individuals who have sustained mild TBIs (including athletes). He has received research


                                                                            D
funding from several test publishing companies, including ImPACT Applications, Inc., CNS Vital

Signs, and Psychological Assessment Resources (PAR, Inc.). He has received research funding as




                            EP
a principal investigator from the National Football League, and salary support as a collaborator

from the Harvard Integrated Program to Protect and Improve the Health of National Football




                              TE
League Players Association Members. DT serves as a consultant for REACT Neuro, Inc.

Christopher Levi serves as a consultant neurologist to the National Rugby League (NRL) providing

a pro bono second opinion to current players regarding concussion assessment and management

for the player's club doctor. Gary Strangman has received pilot research funding from the Harvard

Football Player's Health Study, funded through the National Football League Players Association.

               C
  C
A
Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 ABSTRACT

Purpose: To investigate how four types of successfully executed, legal front-on, one-on-one torso

tackles influence the tacklers’ and ball carriers’ inertial head kinematics. Methods: A total of 455

successful front-on, one-on-one torso tackle trials completed by 15 rugby-code players using three-

dimensional motion capture were recorded. Tackles differed with respects to the height of the

contact point on the ball carrier’s torso. A series of mixed general linear models were conducted.


                                                                            D
Results: The tackler sustained the highest peak resultant linear (p<0.001) and angular (p<0.01)

head accelerations when contacting the lower torso to execute a ‘dominant’ tackle compared to




                            EP
mid or upper torso, although these latter tackle types had the lowest ball carrier inertial head

kinematics. When executing a ‘smother’ tackle technique, a significant decrease in peak resultant




                              TE
linear head acceleration was observed with a vertical ‘pop’ then lock action employed, compared

to the traditional upper torso tackling technique (p<0.001). Conclusions: Modifying the tackler’s

engagement with a ball carrier’s torso, with respect to height and technical execution, alters the

inertial head kinematics of the tackler and the ball carrier. The traditional thinking about optimal

tackle technique, as instructed, may need to be re-evaluated with the mid-torso a potential

               C
alternative target contact height, while changes in tackle execution may be relatively protective for

tacklers when executing either a ‘dominant’ or ‘smother’ tackle. This study provides critical

  C
scientific evidence to underpin revised coaching tackling technique interventions that might



A
enhance player safety. Tackles in which the tackler contacts the ball carrier around the mid torso

region, rather than lower torso, produce the lowest acceleration, and thus may contribute to

reducing head injury risk for the tackler.



Key Words: MOTION CAPTURE; HEAD; CONCUSSION; BIOMECHANICS




Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 INTRODUCTION

        The rugby codes are popular international collision sports. There are 6.1 million rugby

union players globally, including 3.9 million in Europe, 1.8 million in Rugby North America, and

1.1 million in Oceania (1). Numerous physical collisions (2) occur in game play, in which the

defensive players (called the tacklers) attempt to prevent the attacking player (called the ball

carrier) from scoring. Most elite-level rugby league players perform an average of 11 to 30 tackles


                                                                            D
per player per game (3), with some players performing up to 54 tackles per player per game (4).

Elite rugby union players typically perform between 4 and 14 successful tackles per game (5).




                            EP
        The tackle event has the greatest risk for concussion (6-11). Approximately 15.4 [95% CI




                              TE
9.5 to 21.3](12) to 20.4 (11) concussions occurred per 1,000 player match hours in professional

rugby union, and approximately 14.8 [95% CI 9.6 to 23.0](8) in professional rugby league (13).

Online coaching instruction of safer tackling techniques and for reducing concussion risk is offered

by many rugby code governing bodies [e.g., the National Rugby League (NRL) Tackle Safe (14)

(www.playrugbyleague.com/), RugbySmart (15) (www.rugbysmart.co.nz/), and BokSmart (16)

               C
(www.boksmart.com)]. The evidence informing the content of these injury reduction programmes



  C
to reduce concussion risk is limited (17). The programmes are also often based on expert opinion

rather than empirical evidence (16), and as a result, the tackling coaching content taught within



A
these programmes is informed largely by coaching insight and not scientific evidence. It remains

unknown whether or not the content underpinning these tackle interventions results in safer

tackling and promotes player safety. For example, the evidence underpinning the NRL Tackle Safe

(14) program is based on a small study with elite rugby union players (18) (not rugby league

players). The manual identifies a mid-level injury danger area (i.e., ‘orange zone’) when the tackler




Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 contacts the ball carrier at the mid torso (between the ball carrier’s top of pelvis and base of

chest/pectorals), but the safest area or ‘green zone’ is claimed to be when the tackler contacts the

ball carrier on the lower torso, the hip area. This colour zone system is not supported by recent

evidence in professional rugby league (19), where the lowest propensity for HIAs was when the

tackler contacts the ball carrier’s torso (i.e., mid-torso), and the highest propensity (excluding rare

events with a low incidence e.g. boot) and most frequent impact sites are when the tackler contacts


                                                                            D
the torso either too high (i.e., upper torso, or above the sternum/chest) or low (i.e., hip area). This

suggests that the NRL Tackle Safe program (14) may incorrectly identify the safest contact area,




                            EP
and that a reassessment of tackle education based on this colour zone system is warranted.




                              TE
        Despite 95% of concussions in professional rugby league occurring during the tackle (20),

the mechanistic understanding of how tackling technique influences head impact is poorly

understood. During a tackle, impulsive forces (incurred through rapid acceleration and

deceleration) are applied either directly or indirectly to the head, transferring forces to the brain.

These forces can result in a concussion by placing strain on tether points within the brain that may

               C
lead to axonal stress, neuroinflammation, and a neurometabolic cascade (21), that may display as



  C
post-concussion symptoms. These impulsive forces repetitively sustained but that do not lead a

concussion diagnosis (i.e., sub-concussive impact) (22) including from tackling (23) are postulated



A
to be linked to neurological issues, though emerging evidence remain inclusive to date (22).

Whether the injury mechanism is a single event or culminative incidents, reducing the magnitude

of inertial head kinematics of a single tackle or across hundreds of tackles will both achieve an

effect to reduce the risk of concussion when tackling regardless of either mechanism.




Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
         Accurate in-game three-dimensional (3D) tackling methodologies to measure 3D head

kinematics do not currently exist (24). In the laboratory, 3D retroreflective motion analysis is the

gold standard for measuring 3D movement. It provides an understanding of 3D head kinematics

during the tackle and provides an opportunity to examine the risks of head impact associated with

various tackle techniques. However, the 3D retroreflection motion analysis tackle technique

literature measured in the laboratory is emerging (24). The ball carrier has previously been found


                                                                            D
to experience greater changes in head angular velocity and angular acceleration in one-on-one,

front-on, tackles in a upper torso, compared to a low (25) or mid/low torso (26) tackle height.




                            EP
        The objective of this study was to investigate how four types of successfully executed,




                              TE
legal front-on, one-on-one torso tackles influence the tackler’s and ball carrier’s inertial head

kinematics. It was hypothesised that the tackle techniques (i.e., the Dominant, Torso & Stick (DTS)

and the Smother Ball, Pop & Lock (SLP), described subsequently) that adhere most closely to

tackles with the lowest propensity for HIAs (i.e., mid-torso)(19, 27) would result in significantly

decreased peak head linear and angular acceleration for the tackler compared to hip area contact

               C
(Dominant NRL, DNRL) or upper torso area (Smother NRL, SNRL).



  C
METHODS



A
Participants

        Amateur or semi-professional healthy, uninjured, male, adult rugby league or rugby union

players (n = 15) were recruited from grade competitions. The player characteristics of interest

included: sport played (i.e., rugby league or rugby union), participant history in the sport(s) (i.e.,

playing experience in years played), and highest competition level played. At the time of data




Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 collection, each participant’s age, current competition level, and playing position(s) were recorded.

It was deemed a sample size of 14 participants was sufficient based on using previous published

data of the tacklers’ trunk flexion angle at contact when performing an upper and lower torso tackle

(28). The power calculation was determined for two-tailed t-tests with an error probability and

statistical power of 95% using G*Power software (29). Each participant provided written,

informed consent prior to their participation. The University of Newcastle Human Research Ethics

Committee (H-2017-0285) approved the study design and methodology.
                                                                            D
Experimental Procedures


                            EP
        Each data collection session involved two participants, one initially allocated the ball




                              TE
carrier role, and the other participant the tackler role. Participants provided informed consent,

completed a questionnaire of their sporting participation, and then their anthropometric

measurements were recorded for later input into a mathematical model (i.e., body mass, height,

and pelvis, xyphoid, and chest depths). Standing in the anatomical position, a static measurement

of both participants was recorded. The expert coach guided participants to perform a set of 10 trials

               C
of one of four different one-on-one, front-on, torso tackle techniques (see Supplemental Digital



  C
Content 1, Supplemental Figure 1, Schematic diagram of data collection of the 80 trials performed

within a session, http://links.lww.com/MSS/C569) (30). The NRL coaching manual (31) was



A
followed to guide the instruction of two tackling techniques where the tackler’s shoulder contacted

the upper torso (SNRL) or hip area (DNRL) of the ball carrier, respectively. The other two tackling

techniques were novel variations of the NRL tackles. They involved tacklers being instructed to

modify their actions during the contact with the ball carrier: (i) with the tackler lowering the

vertical height of his body position and then performing a vertical ‘pop up’ action that reorients




Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 the motion of the ball carrier into an upward direction (SLP); and (ii) by marginally increasing the

contact height from hip area to mid-torso and redirecting the ball carrier into a vertical and

backward direction (DTS).



        A set of either DNRL or SNRL tackles were always completed first, in a counterbalanced

order. Then participants performed a set of the modified tackle technique (DTS or SLP). Each set


                                                                            D
consisted of five dominant shoulder engagements by the tackler, followed by five trials of non-

dominant shoulder side engagements. This was implemented in this study due to ambiguous




                            EP
evidence as to whether dominant and non-dominant shoulder engagement alters tackle technique

(32, 33).




                              TE
        The expert coach instructed the participants on how to perform the specific technique

correctly, prior to participants engaging in the 10 trials of that technique. Several familiarisation

trials of that technique were performed with coaching feedback delivered. The coach evaluated

every tackle repetition and deemed it successful if, in his assessment, the correct technique had

               C
been executed. Reasons for rejection of a tackle attempt included if the tackler’s head was not on

the side of the ball carrier’s body (right shoulder side tackle, left side of ball carrier’s body) or the

  C
ball carrier was holding the ball on the incorrect side (Figure 1).



A       After the participants completed the 40 tackle trials (4 types, 10 trials per type), the roles

of the participants were reversed (i.e., the tackler became the ball carrier and vice-versa), another

static trial in the anatomical position was performed, followed by another 40 (4 types, 10 of each)

tackling trials. The total experimental protocol lasted approximately three hours.




Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 Expert Coach

        The expert coach for this study was a recently retired dual international rugby league and

rugby union representative player, with junior and senior rugby league and rugby union coaching

experience. This expert coach developed the non-traditional front-on tackle technique (SLP, DTS)

employed in this study. All sessions were attended by the expert coach who gave coaching

Tackling Trials


                            EP
        Every trial started with the ball carrier and tackler in a stationary position, ~4 metres apart.




                              TE
To standardise the approach speed, thereby limiting the confounding factor of player speed (10,

34), the participants were instructed to simultaneously run towards each engaging in contact at

80% game intensity, while each player speed was measured using the three-dimensional motion

caption system. This instruction led to a slow tackle speed (as per the definition of walking or

jogging into the tackle).

               C

than ground contact, causes most tackle injuries (35); as well as (ii) the injury risk for the



A
participants that is associated with the skin mounted retroreflective markers impacting with the

ground. As a result, tackles in this study were done at slower speed with less force (i.e., 80% game

intensity) than would typically occur in field situations in training and matches. The tackle surface

was a 20 m2 matted surface [1000 x 1000 x 40 mm jigsaw mat underlay, 2000 x 1000 x 40 mm

 Tatami Judo mat (Southern Cross Mats, Sydney, NSW & Melbourne, Victoria)]. Rest periods were

30 seconds between trials, and ~5 minutes rest between each new technique set of 10 trials.



        The National Rugby League (NRL) Coaching Manual (31) and Tackle Safe program (14)

outline the technique instruction for the traditional, one-on-one, front-on, torso tackle. Detailed

within these manuals is instruction on how tacklers should be as upright as possible when


                                                                            D
approaching the tackle, then bend their knees while keeping their shoulders higher than hip level

to drop their body position as they are about to execute the tackle. It outlines that tacklers should




                            EP
use their shoulder to make the contact, and position their head to the ball carrier’s side, and

maintain alignment of their neck with the spine by keeping their head up and straight. To take the




                              TE
ball carrier to the ground, the instructional manual outlines the tackler should use a strong leg drive

as well as use the ball carrier’s momentum. Tackle height in accordance with previous research

(18) is recommended in the Tackle Safe program (14) and defines torso contact as either ‘green

zone’ (hip area), ‘orange zone’ (mid torso, between the top of pelvis and base of chest/pectorals),

and ‘red zone’ (upper torso, base of chest/pectorals to line of the shoulders). In this study the tackle

               C
height associated with each tackle type were: hip area (DNRL), mid torso (DTS), mid/upper torso



  C
(SLP), and upper torso (SNRL), respectively (Table 1).




A       Table 1 details the categorisation of each of the tackle types, and how, when, and why a

tackler would employ each tackle type within a game is explained in detailed. The purpose of the

two ‘smother’ tackle types (SLP, SNRL) is to wrap up ball carriers to prevent offloading of the

ball, to prevent the ball carriers from using their forearm/ball as a defensive strategy to bump off

the tackler, and to control the ball carrier when taking the tackle to the ground in order to slow the




Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 play the ball. The two variants of the smother tackle in this study differ from one another in the

way the tackler engages in contact to wrap up the ball and ball carrier, and should be employed by

tacklers when they are on the ball carrying side of the ball carrier. In contrast, the strategy when

performing the two ‘dominant’ tackle instructions (DTS, DNRL) is to bring the ball carrier to the

ground to enable the tackler and defensive team a longer duration to get back onside for the next

play of the ball. The key differences between these dominant strategies are contact height and the


                                                                            D
angle of the force application by the tackler (Table 1). Figure 1 outlines a tackle matrix that

describes when tacklers should execute a dominant tackle (i.e., when the tackler is on the non-ball




                            EP
carrying side of the ball carrier) or a smother tackle (i.e., when the tackler is on the ball carrying

side of the ball carrier) in a game situation.

carrier participants on each of their heads, forearms, upper arms, hands, trunk, pelvis, thighs,

shanks, and feet. A 15 Oqus 700+ camera optoelectronic motion capture system (300 Hz; data

               C
collection volume 10 m x 10 m x 6 m) using Qualisys Track Manager software (v.2018.1, Qualisys



  C
AB, Göteborg, Sweden) recorded the full body three-dimensional kinematic of both participants

for each tackle trial. To adhere to the Nyquist sampling theorem, the sampling rate in this study



A
was determined by spectral analysis (37) of 3D head linear and angular acceleration that indicated

that the median frequency in which that 99% of the data occurs below was 49 Hz.

the three-dimensional data analysis. The raw kinematic data was interpolated with a cubic spline

digital filter prior to calculating kinematic variables. An 18 Hz cut-off frequency was determined

by performing a residual analysis (37) of the raw 3D position of head markers with a median

frequency of 12 Hz (range 9 to 14 Hz) reported from the analysis. The segmental masses and

inertial properties were modelled as per the protocol of Schaefer et al. (2019) (36). To calculate

the tackler and ball carrier. These stages were defined according to the procedures outlined in

2D video analysis, where it is assessed by the thigh relative to trunk (pelvis and thorax treated as

single segment). When identifying how the tacklers executed the lower torso height in the DNRL

technique compared to the SNRL technique, the tacklers did not alter their knee or hip flexion,

however, tacklers increased their trunk-pelvis joint angle by lowering their trunk segment relative

to the ground. In these participants, the tacklers only decreased their tackle height by increasing

               C
their trunk flexion, not their knee or hip flexion. As such, caution is warranted on how researchers



  C
quantify body position prior to and at contact.




A
Understanding linear versus angular head acceleration

        Acceleration of the skull causes rapid deformation of brain matter that is thought to be the

likely cause of concussion (44). This makes intuitive sense, because the impulsive forces (incurred

through a rapid acceleration and deceleration) applied either directly or indirectly to the head

during a tackle, transfer forces through the head to the brain. Those forces can result in a




Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 concussion by placing strain on tether points within the brain that may lead to axonal stress,

neuroinflammation, and a neurometabolic cascade (21). This study observed that head linear

acceleration was significantly different between all tackling instructions, and angular acceleration

only differed in the DNRL. Due to anatomical constraints of these tether points on the brain, when

the skull decelerates the brain’s center of mass will continue to move but the tethering will cause

the brain to rotate (44). This is why brain angular acceleration can occur with only linear


                                                                            D
acceleration of the skull when a mild deceleration of the head is applied (44), and thus both head

linear and angular acceleration are important to measure. Reducing the magnitude of inertial head




                            EP
kinematics of a single tackle or across hundreds of tackles will both achieve an making tackling

safer regardless of either concussion injury mechanism of either an acute event (i.e., direct head




                              TE
impact) or from sub-concussive impacts (i.e., indirect head impact). Recent attempts have been

made to accurately quantify and monitor a player’s in-game exposure to direct and indirect head

impacts in collisions sports via accelerometry (49, 50). These devices use linear acceleration

magnitude threshold of >5G (51) or ≥10G (49, 50, 52) to identify an impact event. These thresholds

are well above this current study’s average peak linear acceleration magnitude reported but are not

               C
too dissimilar to a recent in-game study of professional rugby league players tackling [linear

(median 7.1 G, Q1 = 5.2 G, Q3 =9.9 G); and angular acceleration (median = 0.6 krad/s2, Q1 = 0.4

  C
krad/s2, Q3 = 0.9 krad/s2)]. Caution is advised when comparing different methodological



A
approaches of measuring (53) and filtering (24) head impact data (i.e., head inertial kinematics)

and another confounding issue is the ambigious threshold of head impact data (i.e., head inertial

kinematics) that may cause concusssion. It is recommended that future observational or

interventional research investigating different tackle types measure both 3D head linear and

angular accleration using 3D motion capture and wearable sensors simiulataneously to clarify our




Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.

this study and should be the subject of future research to explore in detail if there is a risk that

when the tackler is deemed to incorrectly execute the tackle it produces undesirable inertial head

kinematics. This may have implications for the global head injury risk in dynamic situations where

tacklers do make errors, and should be a subject of future research.



Limitations

Due to limitations to the current study, these results can only be considered as preliminary




                            EP
and require replication in larger sample sizes. Categorization of the unsuccessful tackles by the

two experts as well as the expert coach potentially leading the participants when instructing the




                              TE
techniques in this study is likely to create a risk of bias because some tackling techniques may

produce higher inertial head kinematics when unsuccessful. Future research should thus explore

tackle success in different tackle types, with a focus on outcomes when tackles are unsuccessful.



        Our findings may not translate to tackles involving more than one tackler, differing

               C
approach direction, playing position or experience, player skill level, age, or tackles that are



  C
completed by taking the ball carrier to ground. Further, the artificial laboratory environment (as

opposed as game environment) may have influenced the ball carrier’s and tackler’s ability to



A
perform the various tackle techniques. The study only investigated a slow tackle speed; therefore,

it remains unknown if altering tackling speed prior to contact changes tackling technique.

Furthermore, the experimental tackles were not completed to the ground, and that could further

reduce the generalizability of findings to actual game play. The study design does not enable any

further investigation of the durability of the behavioral modification (i.e., the robustness of the




Copyright © 2022 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 various tackle techniques) over longer periods of time, or the transfer of the behavioral

modification to match play conditions. Injury history in the subjects was not recorded, so,

secondary analyses could not be conducted to determine if previous injury influenced any of the

participants’ motion.



CONCLUSIONS


                                                                            D
        Head inertial accelerations can be modified in a front-on, one-on-one tackle, at slow speed

within a single session by instructing tacklers to change the torso contact height on the ball carrier




                            EP
and modifying the way they engage in player contact. The inclusion of a tackle specific coaching

instruction training program to alter the impulse forces to the head (i.e., head inertial kinematics)




                              TE
during the tackle may be a viable concussion reduction strategy.

 "evidenceSummary":"Laboratory study in which 15 healthy, uninjured male amateur or semi-professional rugby league and union players performed 455 successful front-on, one-on-one torso tackles at 80% game intensity, recorded with 3D motion capture.    "doi":"10.1249/MSS.0000000000002931",
   "abstract":"The authors used 3D motion capture to examine how four legal front-on, one-on-one torso tackles affected the head kinematics of tacklers and ball carriers, using 455 successful trials from 15 rugby players. The tackler had the highest peak head accelerations when contacting the lower torso, and a modified smother tackle reduced tackler linear head acceleration compared with the traditional upper-torso smother.",
   "tldr":"In a lab study of slow front-on tackles, contacting the hip area produced the highest tackler head accelerations, while a modified smother tackle with a pop-and-lock action produced lower tackler linear head acceleration. Mid-torso contact may lower tackler head loads, but it shifts more load to the ball carrier.",
   "methods":"Laboratory experimental study with a within-player design. Fifteen healthy male rugby players, paired in sessions, each completed 10 trials of each of four tackle instructions (dominant NRL, dominant torso and stick, smother NRL, and smother ball pop and lock) at 80% game intensity, with roles reversed. Full-body 3D motion capture (300 Hz) was used, and mixed general linear models compared peak resultant linear and angular head accelerations across instructions.",
   "findings":"For tacklers, the dominant NRL (hip-area) tackle produced significantly higher peak linear and angular head accelerations than the other three instructions (linear p less than 0.001; angular p between 0.003 and 0.013). The smother ball, pop and lock tackle had lower tackler linear head acceleration than the smother NRL tackle, and lower tackler angular head acceleration than both smother NRL and dominant torso and stick. For ball carriers, the dominant NRL tackle produced the smallest peak linear and angular head accelerations, and the pop-and-lock tackle produced higher ball-carrier accelerations than the smother NRL and dominant torso and stick tackles.",
   "limitations":"The abstract says mid and upper torso tackles produced the lowest ball-carrier head kinematics, but the results and discussion say the hip-area tackle did, so this report follows the results. The study had 15 players, slow tackles, no ground contact, one expert coach, and 145 of 600 trials removed as unsuccessful, which may bias the findings. Injury history was not recorded, and the authors note that the behaviour change was tested only in one session.",
   "practicalImplications":"Coaches can consider mid-torso contact as a target for dominant tackles, since the hip-area tackle gave the highest tackler head accelerations in this lab setting. The authors note a trade-off, because the ball carrier's head loads rise with higher contact, so the change needs testing in match conditions before it is adopted.",
   "athleteDev":"The study supports coaching tacklers to keep the head up and forward, keep the back straight and put the head outside the ball carrier's shoulder. The pop-and-lock smother variant lowered tackler linear head acceleration in slow, expert-coached trials, so it can be practised in controlled training before higher-speed use.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable. The study measures head kinematics in healthy players during slow simulated tackles and does not assess concussion, recovery or return-to-play decisions."
